name: San'ani Arabic
confidence_why: Watson's 2002 weight-sensitive stress algorithm for San'ani Arabic is matched by Rossi's 1939 grammar and by Naïm-Sanbar's 1994 study, which reconciles the one reported divergence, Diem's 1973 stressed heavy finals in words like ḥādirīn, as connected-speech versus pausal placement rather than a different system.

catalog_quote: (8) San'ani stress algorithm (a) Stress the rightmost non-final CVV or CVG syllable. Examples: makātib 'offices', ... ṣābūn 'soap', xārijīn 'going out m.pl.', ... musajjilatī 'my recorder', hākaḏahā 'like this', sāfart 'I/you m.s. travelled', dawwart 'I/you m.s. looked for'. (b) Otherwise stress a final CVVC/CVCC syllable. Examples: darast 'I/you m.s. learnt', ʔabsart 'I/you m.s. saw', gambart 'I/you m.s. sat', ... banāt 'girls'. (c) Otherwise stress the rightmost non-final CVC syllable up to the antepenultimate. Examples: laflaf 'he collected', maklaf 'woman', madrasih 'school', maklafih 'his woman' (d) Otherwise stress the leftmost CV syllable. Examples: katab 'he wrote', darasat 'she learnt', ragabatih 'his neck', maktabatī 'my library'. (e) Stress final CVV in disyllabic adjectives or di- or trisyllabic verbs in the imperfect. Examples: yifʕalū 'they m. do', ṭarī 'fresh'. In contras…

new_statements.quote: Dans les dissyllabes l'accent porte sur la syllabe finale: 1 — si elle est lourde (CV̄C ou CVCC) [...] 2 — si elle présente une voyelle "étymologiquement" longue [...] 3 — dans les dissyllabes munis du suffixe *-at [...] En dehors de ces cas, l'accent frappe la syllabe initiale [...] Les trisyllabes [...] montrent le rôle privilégié de la syllabe pénultième, pour l'établissement de la place de l'accent. Celle-ci est toujours accentuée si sa voyelle est longue, ou brève suivie de consonnes géminées, quelle que soit la nature de la syllabe finale. Autrement, l'accent frappe la syllabe initiale. A la pause, une syllabe finale n'est donc pas accentuée.
new_statements.translation: In disyllables the stress falls on the final syllable: 1 — if it is heavy (CV̄C or CVCC) [...] 2 — if it has an 'etymologically' long vowel [...] 3 — in disyllables carrying the suffix *-at [...] Apart from these cases, the stress falls on the initial syllable [...] Trisyllables [...] show the privileged role of the penultimate syllable in fixing the place of the stress. It is always stressed if its vowel is long, or short and followed by geminate consonants, whatever the nature of the final syllable. Otherwise the stress falls on the initial syllable. At pause, therefore, a final syllable is not stressed.
new_statements.citation: Naïm-Sanbar, Samia. 1994. Contribution à l'étude de l'accent yéménite: le parler des femmes de l'ancienne génération. Zeitschrift für Arabische Linguistik 27: 67-89.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for San'ani Arabic has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Naïm-Sanbar supplies a full weight-sensitive placement rule (final if heavy, else long/geminate penult, else initial, with a pausal/non-pausal split), so it fills the blank rather than contradicting anything. It is consistent with Rossi 1939 §12 (already held by the project from the earlier reading: stress retracts toward the word beginning; final stressed in disyllables only if long with short penult; long penult stressed, else antepenult), which she reinterprets as the pausal system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from syllable weight (long vowel or geminate-closed syllable = heavy) but the author distinguishes two contexts. At pause (utterance-final or hesitation-final): disyllables stress the final if it is CV̄C/CVCC, has an etymologically long vowel, or carries the suffix *-at (-eh), otherwise the initial; trisyllables stress the penult if it is long-vowelled or closed by a geminate, otherwise the initial, and never the final; quadrisyllables stress a CV̄C final, else an antepenult carrying a geminate when the penult is short and the final unstressable. Inside the utterance ('hors pause', pp. 78-80): disyllables stress the final if CV̄C/CVCC, etymologically long *-CV̄ (imperfect and III-w/y verbs), the disjunctive-vowel imperative and a few frozen particles, otherwise the initial; trisyllables stress a heavy final (with a second accent on the initial) and the etymologically long final of imperfects, else a long or geminate-closed penult when the final is unstressable, else the initial; quadrisyllables stress a CV̄C final, else a long penult, else a long or geminate-closed antepenult. She states (p. 87) that within a given form the place of stress is always the same in the same context, and (fn. 71, p. 88) that at the level of the accentual unit the function of stress is culminative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in non-pausal trisyllables with a heavy final 'Cet accent est accompagné d'un deuxième accent, sur la syllabe initiale' (p. 79, e.g. ʾálamâm, sûriyyîn); in quadrisyllables 'La syllabe initiale peut recevoir un accent secondaire' (p. 80, yámaniyyîn); suffixed verb forms may carry two accents (pp. 77, 81, ywálladûwha); after a pause an extra weak initial accent is added to, or replaces, the regular stress (§2.2.2.2, p. 84; p. 88).
new_statements.exceptions: Expressive stress shifts ('accent expressif', §2.2.2.1, pp. 82-84): to the final in balanced CVC.CVC / CVC.CV(C) / CV.CVC disyllables and to a short penult in trisyllables for emphasis; post-pausal initial stress including on the imperfect prefix (§2.2.2.2, p. 84); 'fluctuating' stress in internal-geminate imperfects (yitgáddoʷ vs yitgaddóʷ, p. 80, 'la place de l'accent est donc "fluctuante"'); the suffix -ha is stressed in about a third of pausal tokens (pp. 75-76); II-weak verbs keep initial stress (fn. 39, p. 78); frozen particles ma bəllá, baʿdá, yasʿám, ənnú, kəllú take final stress (p. 79).
new_statements.identity_note: Naïm-Sanbar 1994 describes the speech of unschooled women of the older generation from the old walled city of Sanaa (recordings made at home, 1984-1988), which speakers call a 'second Sanʿani dialect' (lahgah tāniyah hag sanʿa); it is a sociolectal variety of San'ani Arabic (sana1295), not a different language, and the author compares it directly with Rossi 1939, Diem 1973 and Qafisheh 1988 on Sanaa Arabic generally.

readall_conflicts: Only one work was in scope and it does not contradict the (empty) catalog rule. Inside the work, Naïm-Sanbar reports a disagreement among earlier descriptions of Sanaa Arabic: Rossi 1939 and Qafisheh 1988 privilege the penult and let stress retract toward the beginning of the word despite heavy syllables (e.g. hâdirin, kátabên, hawânit), whereas Diem 1973 makes a heavy final (CV̄C/CVCC) obligatorily stressed (hâdirîn, katabên, hawânît) (pp. 69-70, 86). She resolves this (pp. 86-87) as two contexts rather than two systems: Diem describes word stress inside the utterance ('hors pause'), Rossi and Qafisheh the stronger stress at pause, where a final syllable is never stressed except in disyllables; the forms on which all three agree (kibâr, mátar, yúrgud, sîrû, mádraseh, wâhideh, tallâgeh) are exactly those where the two contexts give the same result. Rossi 1939 §12 (held by the project from the previous pass) also notes that the rules are not absolute and that stress depends on emphasis and position in the sentence; this matches her 'irregular' expressive and post-pausal shifts.

Nei trisillabi l'accento sta sulla terzultima sillaba se la penultima è breve, sulla penultima se questa è lunga ... Nota 2.
